newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Few live dream of Ukraine constitution one year on.
newsitem.headline: Few live dream of Ukraine constitution one year on.

text.p: Ukraine cast off another chain of its post-Soviet inheritance by approving a constitution a year ago on Saturday, but so far only a few are living the dream of economic freedom it wrote into law.
One year on, a non-payments crisis has made a mockery of its promises of a right to work, to food and to pay for all, while a third of the population of 51 million earns $30 to $50 a month.

Living standards in Ukraine are still way behind those in neighbouring Russia, which came 67th in the latest United Nations' index measuring life expectancy, educational achievement and standard of living in 175 countries.
With millions of state workers going unpaid for months and only 0.6 percent of the population earning more than $150 a month, Ukraine came only 95th on the index.

Nowhere is the gap between rich and poor more evident than in big cities like Kiev, where street kids beg money from the rich business class as they step out of flash Western cars, brandishing mobile phones and wearing smart designer suits.
The economic crisis has sparked a brain drain among what is seen as a well-educated population, with many of the brightest and best taking off for central Europe and beyond to earn a decent wage.

"Of course it's hard. It's hard to see your friends, relatives, really talented people you studied with having to go to Poland or the Czech Republic just to earn a few pennies," said Nikolai, a leading television executive working in Kiev.
The official statistics conceal about 60 percent of the economy which is "in the shadow", or undeclared, with many people improving their lot by subsidising pitiful wages with unofficial earnings.
But the weak go unprotected, like dozens of invalid coal miners who picketed behind barriers near the president's administration this week to demand 15 months' unpaid allowances.

Grey-faced and worn down by years underground in the Donetsk coal-mining region, they sat down outside the constitutional court which since it started work on January 1 has had 2,000 complaints -- mostly from citizens demanding unpaid wages.

"People don't understand that they can demand their rights from an ordinary court. But for that they need a good lawyer, and most people cannot afford that," Volodymyr Shlyaposhnikov, the court's press secretary, told Reuters.

"They are not used to the legal system. They think the constitutional court will help them. The Soviet system taught them to turn to the Party's highest organs, so they turn to us, because they think we are the highest authority," he said.
Outside, the miners, who get about 60 hryvnias ($30) a month when they do get paid, were getting angrier. "Some of us spent 30 years down the pit, but now no one needs us," one said.
"Constitution? Constitution?" spat another wizened man with a yellowish face. "They only passed it for themselves."

Left-leaning deputies in parliament who have blocked this year's budget for months as they feel it does not offer enough social protection also on Thursday invoked the constitution -- the same document which set the budget deadline at January 1.
Olexander Yakovenko, a leading communist, read a statement from agrarians, socialists and communists demanding President Leonid Kuchma's impeachment. It said:

"Ukraine's new budget confirms the final collapse of its economy and violates the constitution, in particular its social guarantees. A majority of the Ukrainian people will be even worse-off once the budget is passed...The country is on the brink of catastrophe."

The constitution does allow parliament to impeach the president in theory but in practice it would only be possible in extreme cases as it needs the support of 75 percent of parliament, plus the supreme court and the constitutional court.
